With consent, `clanker_personal_read(fields)` returns only the requested saved primary fields and lists required fields that are missing. It accepts no owner, profile, credential handle or website-supplied field name. Live membership, authenticated requester, private DM/task route and delegated-execution checks apply. Shared-channel calls move into the linked owner-only private task before any values can be returned. The read never resolves owned or invited credential records. ## Form handling and disclosure Clanker maps the returned data to actual visible controls using native Kernel snapshots and input actions. English label regexes are not required for this consented path. Native `browser_type` supports ordinary replacement fill and a character insertion mode for incremental input. The pinned driver uses native `Input.insertText` for printable characters; it does not promise keydown events. Command success alone does not prove that a controlled form accepted the value. Before character insertion, the wrapper checks that the exact referenced field is empty. A rejected or unconfirmed clear stops insertion; private readback and transport error payloads are excluded from diagnostics and tool responses. Browser ownership, page guards, lease fences and Kernel-only routing continue to apply. Reading or filling grants no purchase, signup, messaging or account-change authorization; automatic payment remains disabled. Personal values remain registered for presentation/log redaction and public Slack updates. The private model tool result and subsequent tool arguments may persist in private conversation history and be sent to the configured model provider. Revoking consent blocks future reads; it does not erase data already received by the model or its conversation history. Existing encrypted primary storage remains encrypted. No central secret-redaction exception is added. ## Verification The canonical runners passed 380 checks across 18 files, including owner consent, field minimization, private routing, revocation, encrypted persistence, actual tool dispatch and private transport diagnostics. A real Kernel synthetic phone field accepted native incremental insertion; a rejected controlled clear safely refused further typing. Full address and merchant acceptance remain unverified. See [the verification evidence](../../verification/evidence/2026-10-08-consented-personal-model-access.md) for the partial live proof and activation status. # Vault invitations and requester authorization The vault has one **Invite to vault** button. The owner chooses a current Slack member, checks which saved logins, API keys and payment cards to share, then confirms use of only that selection on their behalf. Nothing is checked for a new member, and credentials added later stay private. **People with access** groups each member's shared credentials; **Edit access** reopens the checklist with that member's existing selection, and **Remove** revokes their access. The member sees **Shared with you** in their vault. An invitation takes effect immediately. When the selection adds credentials, Clanker sends one private Slack DM to the recipient with the sharer's Slack mention, the number of newly shared credentials, and an **Open vault** button. The message includes no credential titles, identifiers, grant handles, secrets, or authenticated link tokens. Unchanged saves and removal-only edits send no DM. The vault confirms Slack delivery or reports that delivery could not be confirmed; access remains saved in either case. Delivery is bounded to ten seconds and is not retried automatically. Slack's own notification settings control whether the DM also produces a push notification. The saved credential remains in the owner's encrypted native vault. The guest receives a grant handle and metadata, not a copied vault entry. This implements explicit delegation. It does **not** establish that the reported Gmail disclosure is fixed in the running system. The gateway has not been reloaded, no real invitation has been created, and the consumer browser provider's isolation and cookie-deletion behavior remain unverified. ## Permission boundary Slack OIDC establishes the owner of the vault web session. Owner and workspace come from that session, never request-body fields. CSRF and exact-origin checks cover invite and revoke. Only native items in that owner's vault can be invited; guests cannot pass an invited handle to create another invitation. A durable grant binds workspace, owner, recipient and selected credential. Saving a member's checklist validates the entire selection and applies all permission additions/removals in one database transaction. Invalid or foreign items cause no partial changes. Still-selected credentials retain their grant handles; unchecked credentials and their pending approvals are revoked before browser cleanup. Selecting credentials grants no wildcard access to the vault. Its identity binding includes kind, origin, account identifier and creation time. The runtime resolves that grant for the authenticated requesting member, checks current membership of both parties, and verifies the selected native item still exists with that binding. An unrelated native handle, another member's grant, a removed or changed account, or a disabled member is denied. Reinvitation after revocation produces a new grant handle. These are credential-use permissions. A login can provide the full website account access available to that login; an API key can provide the permissions the service gives that key. The implementation does not impose a new read-only role inside either service. Preventing onward grants is an application rule; it is not a guarantee that an authorized recipient cannot copy account data or that a third-party browser provider cannot access an entered credential. ## Execution Logins fill the requester's supervised local browser, after exact origin and supported-field inspection. The selected owner password is supplied by the trusted backend, without switching the active Hermes home to the owner. Owner TOTP or a hosted owner-only code form can satisfy verification. The one-use code is consumed in the original requester's task, and automatic resume retains that requester's source, home and DM. API requests use `clanker_api_request`: the backend adds the owned or invited key to a supported authentication header. Calls accept relative paths on the saved HTTPS origin, reject authentication/Host/Cookie overrides, reject private or local DNS addresses, pin the connection to a resolved public IP, and verify TLS against the original hostname. Redirects do not forward authentication. Request and response sizes are limited. Key values are registered for redaction and scrubbed from responses. Synthetic transport tests verify these restrictions; no real external API operation was performed for this change. Cards use only the requester's supervised local checkout. An invitation lets the member request a purchase; each exact purchase still needs the **card owner's** hosted approval and current CVV. The owner sees merchant, order, total, checkout text and requester. Approval does not transfer the task to the owner. The handler rechecks the original browser, task, conversation and checkout, consumes approval and CVV before fill/submission, and refuses replay. Submitted is not paid; the merchant receipt must be checked. Unsupported payment frames, wallets, subscriptions and bank approval retain their existing limits. ## Revocation and cookies Revocation is committed before cleanup and cancels pending delegated code/card approvals. Secret-bearing browser use is recorded before handoff, with an atomic active-grant check. This covers a revoke racing between handle resolution and the usage record. Work already in flight may finish before interruption; the implementation cannot undo earlier disclosures or completed external actions. For local Chromium, revoke interrupts the original requester task, closes their private browsers and deletes their Chromium cookie profile under the guest execution lock. Cleanup conservatively removes all of that recipient's private browser state, including sessions used for other valid grants. It preserves the owner's browser and native vault. An active grant can be used again in a fresh guest browser after cleanup. API requests have no reusable browser cookies. If cleanup fails, the grant remains revoked and the recorded usage keeps future browser/terminal execution blocked. The web UI shows **cleanup pending** and offers retry. **People with access** also exposes orphan invitations whose native credential was removed, so that member's access can still be removed or cleanup retried. Consumer Browser Tool exposes task stop but no reviewed cookie/session deletion operation. Its stop result now reports `profile_retained: null` (unknown), correcting the previous unsupported claim of cookie deletion. A required purge stops the task, keeps a blocked tombstone, and returns cleanup pending. Repeated stop/retry does not clear that block. Operator cleanup needs an actual provider deletion/reconciliation capability before a verified reset can be recorded; this implementation does not supply that capability. ## Browser routing and unresolved incident work New cloud state keys include workspace, authenticated requester and resolved home, independent of the short session name or a shared conversation profile. State carries an explicit owner marker. Provider session IDs are recorded with that owner/context, and a recorded collision is refused and quarantined. Legacy state is not silently adopted by the new namespace. Unknown dispatch outcomes retain their retry block. These controls govern Clanker's assignments and known grants. They do not prove a fresh remote browser lacks another account's pre-existing cookies. Provider ownership collisions are detected on acknowledgement, after task dispatch; that check cannot undo observations the provider made before acknowledging. Free-form remote task instructions are not an account-authorization boundary. The reported disclosure therefore still requires tracing and invalidating affected legacy/provider state, a provider-enforced requester isolation and pre-read authorization design, and real two-requester/DM-handoff acceptance. Existing login state alone must never be used as permission. ## Verified locally The canonical Hermes test runner passed **79 tests across five affected files**: invitations, vault, payments, consumer Browser Tool and managed cloud browser. Coverage includes all three credential kinds, owner/recipient/workspace checks, CSRF and forged identity fields, persistence, onward-sharing denial, revoked access, cleanup failure, same session names/shared profile names, recorded provider-session collisions, delegated code and payment resume, origin-bound API requests, TLS/DNS pinning and redirect rejection. Checklist coverage adds multi-credential sharing, atomic rejection without partial permission changes, stable handles for retained credentials, revocation of unchecked items, no automatic sharing of later credentials, and removal of an inactive member. The actual sandboxed Chromium probe exercised A → B → A with two disposable homes: owner login, denial of the owner's raw handle to the guest, invited login fill, owner-only HTTP approval, one guest dummy checkout with an observed dummy receipt, payment replay denial, CVV consumption, no copied guest vault entry, guest cookie-profile removal when the login is unchecked in that member's selection, and preservation of the owner's browser. The same guest task/session can start a fresh browser after cleanup, while the revoked login remains denied and an unrelated active card grant remains listed. Its receipt is [`2026-10-06-invitation-local-browser.json`](../../verification/evidence/2026-10-06-invitation-local-browser.json). The visible UI check uses disposable identities and dummy credentials on loopback. The owner initially selected login and API key; the guest saw those two entries and no card. Edit access restored that checklist; unchecking the login and checking the card made guest reload show only API key and card, with the per-purchase owner-approval label. Desktop and mobile checklists and the member-level sharing list were visually checked. Removing the member through the single member row then made guest reload show no saved or invited access. Earlier per-credential Invite screenshots represent the superseded design. The missing favicon is unrelated to invitation behavior. No mailbox content, real credential, live Slack message, real card charge or production configuration change is used as verification evidence. "}}}

1	# Persistent personal and shared-account browser profiles
     2	
     3	## Finding
     4	
     5	The requested topology is one persistent browser identity for each authorized
     6	Slack member, plus a separate identity for each shared login. The current
     7	workspace has three ready members and one shared Swiggy login, so its intended
     8	steady state is four profiles. Profiles are allocated on use; this is not a
     9	global four-profile limit for future members or shared accounts.
    10	
    11	Read-only inventory on October 11 found 34 provider profiles: 15 retained task
    12	profiles and 19 Managed Auth profiles. All matched local ownership metadata.
    13	The two benchmark participants own 18 and 16 respectively; the third member
    14	has none. Six auth connections still reported authenticated success. Historical
    15	claims and execution directories are not additional live browser profiles.
    16	
    17	Ordinary cleanup also lost useful sessions. In the [earlier Goa
    18	task](https://clanker-global.slack.com/archives/C0C6J277ZNG/p1791715417473369),
    19	the model called `clanker_browser_stop` at 16:27:28 IST; cleanup finished at
    20	16:27:37.611. The auth flow became deleted at 16:27:37.602. Its successful login
    21	had occurred at 16:21:30. The implementation retained canonical private-home
    22	auth flows but deleted the connection and profile for an isolated execution
    23	home. Its saved credential reference survived. This was task cleanup, not a
    24	human logout. The unconditional `profile_retained` response concealed the
    25	distinction.
    26	
    27	## Change
    28	
    29	Browser identity and task execution identity now have separate responsibilities.
    30	Persistent personal keys contain workspace and member identity. Shared keys
    31	contain workspace, credential owner and immutable saved-item identity. After a
    32	login becomes shared, its owner and current authorized recipients select that
    33	same dedicated profile. A shared profile never adopts a whole personal profile.
    34	Current membership, exact credential metadata and current grants are checked
    35	on selection, browser use and immediately before writer dispatch. Task homes,
    36	Slack source bindings, native task IDs, remote browser claims and CDP claims
    37	remain requester-scoped.
    38	
    39	A SQLite reservation permits one writer per profile, across task homes and
    40	browser/auth workers. It is recorded before dispatch and survives process
    41	restart. Unknown dispatch outcomes do not expire into another writer. Confirmed
    42	preflight non-dispatch can release its reservation, and confirmed remote closure
    43	releases an active writer. Cleanup is idempotent without releasing a later
    44	writer. Waiting occurs outside execution-home locks so the preceding task can
    45	finish. Persistent state does not imply live synchronization: [Kernel saves a
    46	complete snapshot and permits one safe writer](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/profiles/concurrency).
    47	
    48	Managed Auth connects multiple site-specific connections to a personal profile,
    49	as supported by [Kernel's Managed Auth contract](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/auth/managed-auth).
    50	Each consuming task selects its own authorized credential handle; the original
    51	flow creator's grant is not authority for a later recipient. Normal task stop
    52	releases task/browser bindings while retaining authenticated profile state.
    53	Explicit account disconnection quarantines residual session state until its
    54	cleanup is reconciled; deleting one site's credential must not silently erase
    55	unrelated sites from the personal profile.
    56	
    57	Private browser startup resolves its profile before selecting vault attachments.
    58	Shared mode attaches only the selected credential's dedicated vault. Public
    59	discovery does not load a member's personal cookies. Revocation closes the
    60	revoked recipient's browsers and clears their task references; it does not
    61	delete the shared profile belonging to the remaining authorized users.
    62	
    63	The [checked migration](2026-10-11-browser-profile-migration.md) preserves two
    64	explicitly reviewed personal profiles and their exact existing connections.
    65	It neither merges cookies nor transfers historical task approval. Remaining
    66	legacy state stays separate pending verified replacement and cleanup review.
    67	A new canonical profile does not recover cookies from an already deleted one.
    68	
    69	Separate startup provisioning creates the two reviewed missing identities:
    70	the third member's empty personal profile and an empty shared Swiggy profile.
    71	Its manifest binds exact principal names, current members, the credential's
    72	metadata hash and the complete active recipient set. Every target is checked
    73	before the first profile POST and again between provider operations. Existing
    74	registry reservations reconcile an uncertain POST by exact-name GET rather
    75	than issuing another creation. This stage creates no browser, login, grant or
    76	credential. Two retained profiles plus two new ones leave 36 physical profiles
    77	until the 32 legacy profiles have been separately cleaned up.
    78	
    79	Both startup stages require the actual gateway process lock, PID and launch
    80	home. Protected outcome receipts contain the manifest hash, current PID and
    81	timestamp. Activation must verify these fresh receipts and Vault availability;
    82	Slack connectivity alone does not establish successful migration.
    83	
    84	## Validation and limits
    85	
    86	Implementation and verification are in progress; this document is not a live
    87	deployment or four-profile inventory claim. Canonical test logs and independent
    88	security review are recorded under
    89	`.local/clanker-qa/findings/persistent-browser-principals/`.
    90	
    91	The registry tests use real SQLite and independent instances. They cover three
    92	personal identities plus one shared identity, cross-user/workspace refusal,
    93	revocation and credential rotation, competing browser/auth writers, unknown
    94	creation reconciliation without another POST, and forged cleanup evidence. A
    95	red/green regression also covers a crash between lease deletion and the
    96	caller's cleanup receipt: replaying the old cleanup cannot release a newer
    97	writer. Browser and Managed Auth integration checks exercise actual runtime
    98	imports against temporary execution homes with provider I/O fixtures.
    99	
   100	The isolated registry/authority suite passes 41 checks. Fifteen writer-handoff
   101	checks cover the uninterrupted browser-to-auth reservation and stale cleanup.
   102	Seventeen provisioning checks cover exact topology, changed grants/credentials,
   103	unknown POST reconciliation, guarded startup and sanitized process-bound
   104	outcomes. Two startup receipt cases failed before their fix; the initial
   105	provisioning-module absence is not a behavioral regression. The combined activation run passed 1,013 checks across 49 files with zero
   106	failures, eight existing expected failures, and no file retries. The exact
   107	file list and log are `activation-tests.json` and `activation-green.log` in
   108	the finding directory. Independent review passed the profile, migration,
   109	provisioning, and scoped-reset boundaries. Live results remain pending.
   110	
   111	Provider login dispatch has no force-clean-session parameter. A fresh login
   112	generation is not proof that an authenticator challenge occurred. Autonomous
   113	TOTP still requires live challenge/completion evidence. Owner-only email/SMS,
   114	push or other external authentication steps remain human actions when the
   115	website actually requires them. None of these local checks changes the
   116	historical benchmark outcomes or establishes 12/12 success.
     1	# Persistent browser profile integration
     2	
     3	## Scope
     4	
     5	The browser profile registry owns durable personal and shared-account identity.
     6	Kernel automation still owns each live browser and CDP connection through its
     7	authenticated requester, execution home and Slack thread. A persistent profile
     8	does not make a browser or Hermes execution home shareable.
     9	
    10	Private startup resolves and authorizes its principal before attaching vaults.
    11	Public discovery uses an anonymous browser without personal cookies or vaults.
    12	Each principal has one durable writer lease, shared by automation and Managed
    13	Auth. Automation waits at most 60 seconds outside the execution-home lock,
    14	allowing the previous task to stop. This is bounded waiting, not a durable FIFO
    15	queue. A trusted gateway may retire an idle browser only after verifying its
    16	exact ownership and excluding pending code forms, approvals, undelivered
    17	resumes and unresolved purchases. Auth connections and unknown dispatches are
    18	never treated as expired browser sessions.
    19	
    20	Normal stop verifies browser closure, releases its exact lease and keeps the
    21	principal profile. Revocation cleanup closes only the recipient's execution
    22	contexts and preserves the shared profile for the remaining authorized users.
    23	Legacy task profiles are quarantined locally for explicit reconciliation; this
    24	change neither adopts nor deletes them. Existing native browser and CDP owner
    25	claims are unchanged.
    26	
    27	## Vault boundaries
    28	
    29	A shared browser attaches only its selected credential's dedicated vault.
    30	The owner and authorized recipients use that same shared principal. Personal
    31	browsers attach their owner's personal vault and unshared dedicated items;
    32	invited vaults are excluded. An owned item is also excluded when an active
    33	grant or a historical shared principal identifies it as shared.
    34	
    35	Hosted fills recheck the current principal and credential. Shared mode refuses
    36	personal-info, direct-item and formatted-value fills before private values are
    37	read or temporary items are created. Only the selected shared login and its
    38	authorized verification flow may fill the shared browser. These controls do
    39	not claim to be general DLP for manually supplied text or website content.
    40	
    41	## Lifecycle regressions
    42	
    43	Two integration failures were reproduced and repaired during implementation:
    44	
    45	- When a new authentication binding replaced the current browser but kept the
    46	  same principal, closing the browser released the idempotently acquired lease.
    47	  Startup now reserves again outside the home lock before creating a replacement.
    48	- Revocation immediately before writer dispatch correctly prevented a browser
    49	  POST but left an unknown-dispatch marker. Known pre-dispatch refusals now clear
    50	  that marker and release only the reserved lease. Actual uncertain provider
    51	  outcomes retain their durable block.
    52	
    53	## Verification
    54	
    55	Canonical local tests use real SQLite, real requester/grant resolution and the
    56	real registry, with fixture Kernel/CDP I/O. Initial integration red was four
    57	failures and one pass. Focused regressions separately reproduced the released
    58	lease, pre-dispatch marker and personal/shared vault-boundary failures.
    59	
    60	- `integration-scope-green.log`: 153 passed, 8 existing expected failures across
    61	  six files, including 18 new integration cases.
    62	- `integration-fill-related-green.log`: 167 passed across personal information,
    63	  saved-login browser recovery, fill dispatch, split OTP and retry authorization.
    64	
    65	Logs are under `.local/clanker-qa/findings/persistent-browser-principals/`.
    66	Saved-login recovery tests now reproduce an actual personal-to-shared profile
    67	switch, because changing an ordinary personal thread must preserve its profile.
    68	All owner, unrelated-refusal and stale-form recovery assertions remain.
    69	
    70	This is local verification. It does not prove deployed cookie persistence,
    71	website login, cart continuity or benchmark completion. No live browser,
    72	production database, remote profile or gateway was changed by these tests.

     1	# Benchmark replay preparation
     2	
     3	## Finding
     4	
     5	The requested evidence campaign must repeat all twelve unchanged benchmark tasks only after the repair campaign honestly completes all twelve. No evidence campaign has started, no replay is enabled, and no Slack screenshot has been captured for it.
     6	
     7	Kernel's current [replay documentation](https://www.kernel.sh/docs/browsers/replays) supports explicit session recording, separate start/stop segments, and MP4 download. The official [Python SDK wire contract](https://github.com/kernel/kernel-python-sdk/blob/main/src/kernel/resources/browsers/replays.py) uses POST `/browsers/{id}/replays`, POST `/browsers/{id}/replays/{replay_id}/stop`, and GET `/browsers/{id}/replays/{replay_id}`. Its options include a duration bound and disabling audio. These sources were checked on 2026-10-11. The documentation calls replay-view URLs sensitive; none are retained in result metadata.
     8	
     9	Neither source documents an authentication-redaction guarantee. A browser restored from an authenticated profile can display private values before its first tool call. Native autofill can precede the Vault fill boundary. Managed Auth uses a separate browser and does not pass through the ordinary fill guard; ordinary private values may also be returned to the model for later native typing. Stopping recording after a DOM inspection cannot undo already-recorded frames. A single pre-fill hook therefore does not establish safe capture.
    10	
    11	## Change
    12	
    13	`runtime/cloud_browser/kernel_replay.py` is standalone preparation, with no production import, browser hook, model tool, CLI command, or activation setting written by this change.
    14	
    15	- `ReplayPlan` is off when the protected backend's `benchmark-replays.json` is absent or disabled. An enabled manifest must be owned by the process user, private to that user, bounded in size and lifetime, and match the exact team, requester, Slack channel, thread root, browser context and provider session. Current ownership is checked against the existing authoritative browser-owner registry. A tester identity or profile alone is insufficient, so concurrent ordinary sessions cannot enter a campaign accidentally.
    16	- Even a valid exact match returns `capture_allowed: false`, reason `auth_exclusion_unavailable`. No manifest flag can override this. Authentication, saved-access and restored-profile sessions remain uncaptured. A future safe boundary needs a separate implementation and review before any runtime capture can start.
    17	- The isolated `ReplayAPI` adapter implements the documented wire contract for synthetic tests. Start is video-only at 10fps, with an explicit duration from 1 to 600 seconds. Mutations never automatically retry. An invalid or lost start response is an unknown outcome, not proof that recording did not begin; no second start should be attempted until reconciled. A failed stop is not completion. The provider duration bound limits such a recording, but is not a privacy guarantee.
    18	- Export streams a bounded MP4 response into a private temporary file and publishes a new immutable local artifact only after successful completion. Redirects are refused. Failed, malformed or oversized downloads leave no partial artifact. Existing artifacts and symlinks are not overwritten. Export returns only a local path, byte count and SHA-256; capability URLs, headers and raw provider error text are excluded.
    19	
    20	The [evidence table](../verification/2026-10-11-benchmark-evidence.md) preserves all twelve initial prompts and the required four columns. Every run ID and artifact is pending. Future Slack images must show the actual exact thread in Aside, with thread identity checked before capture. Exclude auth cards and access links before taking a screenshot; no synthetic conversation rendering or invented screenshot may substitute for Slack evidence. An unavailable safe screenshot or replay stays explicitly unavailable. Authentication intervals are never silently presented as complete coverage.

Review decisions 12 13 1. **Initial transport and host:** retain Socket Mode in one persistent Python gateway container on Cloudflare, provisionally. This draft does not approve spending. 18 19 These are proposals for review. Existing `MOD_HERMES.md` proposes relay; this draft offers runs API as the initial candidate and does not silently amend that document. 20 21 ## 2. Problem and intended experience 22 23 The stock Slack listener and reply code can be useful, but Clanker requires a task to outlive the gateway's current agent invocation and any assigned worker. Receiving ten task events from ten different authorized users must create ten owner/context-scoped tasks. Capacity may run only some immediately; the remainder wait fairly. None share a private Hermes agent, profile mount, browser state or task authority. 24 25 The gateway is one trusted service. Multiple replicas, maximum throughput discovery and load benchmarking are not v1 prerequisites. One service may include transport and trusted control components; it must not execute arbitrary agent code. 26 27 ### Concrete journeys 28 29 | Journey | Required user-visible behavior | 30 | --- | --- | 31 | Private browser task | User DMs a request, sees accepted/queued status, receives useful progress and a verified result in that DM. The assigned worker loads only their authorized context. | 32 | Ten independent users | Ten DM requests become ten distinct tasks tied to the right owners. With a smaller pool, queued users retain their place and eventually receive their own results. | 33 | Shared collaboration | Two admitted participants contribute to one channel thread. They share its authorized conversation context, without loading either participant's private account state. | 34 | Private access during shared work | Shared work identifies a need for Alice's private account. The gateway obtains Alice's authorization privately and creates/links a private task. Private observations return to Alice; sharing selected content requires her exact approval. | 35 | Human input and recovery | A task waits for clarification or a private access form. The worker can be released after a durable checkpoint. Valid input resumes the same task once, even if the prior worker was replaced. | 36 37 ## 3. Responsibilities and boundaries 38 39 | Component | Owns | Does not own | 40 | --- | --- | --- | 41 | Shared gateway | Slack connection, admission, authenticated identity, audience mapping, durable task acceptance, safe progress/replies, owner-bound controls | Browser execution, deciding capacity, decrypting vault secrets in chat, arbitrary agent code | 42 | Scheduler/pool manager | Fair dispatch, profile lease, worker assignment, capacity bounds, clean-worker lifecycle, recovery coordination | Deriving human identity from model text, Slack publication authority | 43 | Isolated worker | Hermes, Browser Use driver, local Chromium, scoped profile/files, run events and checkpoints | Broad Slack/cloud credentials, other profiles, independent destination selection | 44 | Durable context store | Versioned authorized history/browser/files and checkpoints beyond worker lifetime | Treating object keys supplied by agents as access grants | 45 | Trusted vault/access service | Slack OIDC, owner/task/site authorization, secure submission, protected storage, durable access-ready signal | Sending passwords/setup keys through Slack, model inputs or queues | 46 47 The gateway submits an authorized task to the scheduler. Revalidate the permitted destination before delivery; membership/authorization changes suspend affected work for reconciliation. 69 70 **G4. Distinct authorities.** Track requester, resource owner and output audience separately. Worker confinement.** Mount/load exactly the assigned context and its permitted files/browser state. Trusted envelopes 75 76 These are required semantics, not a frozen wire schema. Do not place credentials, broad bearer tokens or secrets in task messages or logs. 87 88 ## 6. Acceptance, deduplication and ordering 89 90 **G6. Durable acceptance before success.** Persist the accepted event and task/dispatch intent before acknowledging a task event. If persistence fails, do not claim acceptance. Keep transport acknowledgement within Slack's three-second budget; worker startup and model calls occur later. Unsupported/no-op events may be acknowledged without creating tasks. 91 92 **G7. Do not collapse an intentional edit or separate user message. Use transport-specific interaction/command identities and make control consumption idempotent. Profile serialization.** Scheduler leases permit one active run per profile, including shared profiles with multiple thread sessions. Preserve accepted turn order within that profile. Fairly service independent contexts under configured capacity; a busy user cannot monopolize all slots. Throughput ceilings and multi-gateway routing are deferred. 97 98 ## 7. Progress, replies and controls 99 100 **G10. Delivery association.** Every progress, clarification, artifact and completion belongs to a task/run and server-selected destination. Socket Mode is inbound transport; replies still use Slack APIs. Workers return events/results to the gateway rather than directly posting to Slack. 101 102 **G11. Restarting the gateway must not launch the browser task merely because its reply was undelivered. Reconcile ambiguous sends where possible; retain unresolved delivery status rather than claiming exactly-once Slack publication. 103 104 **G12. Useful status.** Show accepted/queued state, meaningful progress, waiting reason, completion, cancellation or actionable failure. Coalesce repetitive progress. Do not claim an account action succeeded from a generated answer alone; completion requires worker outcome evidence or an explicit uncertain result. 105 106 **G13. Owner-bound approval.** Validate authenticated clicker against the durable approval owner and current task/run. Bind consequential execution approval to the exact action; changed details require a new request. Private-result sharing approval additionally binds exact content/artifacts and destination audience. Tool permission approval alone is not publication consent. Enforce expiry and single consumption; denied, foreign and replayed decisions cannot resume execution. 107 108 **G14. Cancellation.** An authorized owner may cancel their private task; shared task controls follow an explicit requester/owner policy, proposed as task requester only for v1. Queued cancellation prevents dispatch. Running cancellation reaches the assigned run and revokes further execution authority. Report `cancelling` until stop is observed, and disclose any external action already performed or whose outcome is uncertain. Late callbacks cannot revive a cancelled task. 109 110 ## 8. Clarification text can use its admitted Slack surface; account secrets use the separate secure access flow. An access-ready signal carries a safe handle, never a password. Atomically consume valid input and record readiness once. Reject mismatched/expired/replayed input; input arriving after cancellation does not resume work. 113 114 **G16. Worker release.** A waiting worker may be released only after a durable task/checkpoint transition. Run and approval state held only in process memory cannot justify scale-down. Resuming on another worker re-establishes the pending intent from persisted state; do not assume an old in-memory approval resolver survives replacement. 115 116 **G17. Context persistence.** At task start, load the authorized durable context version. Checkpoint history, browser state and files consistently at defined safe points and before clean release. Use lease/fencing validation for checkpoint publication. Close/flush SQLite and browser state, or use a supported consistent snapshot; copying live files is not established as safe. Never reuse a dirty private worker for another context without verified reset/replacement. 117 118 **G18. Failure classification.** Track accepted, queued, preparing, running, waiting-for-input/approval, cancelling, completed, failed, cancelled and needs-reconciliation states, with durable transition versions. A worker outage makes the current attempt interrupted. Requeue only after reconciling its lease, checkpoint and possible external effects.
